title: Harbor & Pine — Routing v3 demo & pilot terms

chapters.title: Kickoff and recap
chapters.gist: Small talk about peak season and the Kent data Marcus sent; Tom recaps the discovery call and Daniel sets up a demo run on Harbor & Pine's real Kent orders.

chapters.title: Routing v3: dispatch board, constraints and live re-planning
chapters.gist: Daniel shows Routing v3 on last Tuesday's Kent orders: the dispatch board, hours-of-service and dock-window constraints, dispatcher locks, and a 4-second re-solve of about 400 stops after a simulated breakdown.

chapters.title: Samsara and the Oracle TMS
chapters.gist: Daniel explains the Samsara API integration and is candid about the two Oracle TMS options: a nightly SFTP batch that works now but misses intraday changes, or a middleware connector that is near real-time but needs a change-board approval and 4–6 weeks. Elena also presses on the Sep 24 ETA outage.

chapters.title: Pricing, pilot terms and live ETA
chapters.gist: Tom quotes $68/truck/month list and offers a free 6-week, 60-truck Kent pilot converting at $62; Marcus counters with RouteWise at $52. Marcus presses for a live ETA date, Daniel won't give one without Maya, and Tom promises something concrete next week. Next steps: questionnaire back to Elena, pilot proposal by Oct 6, Marcus briefs Dana.

turns.t: Hey Elena. Hi. Is Marcus on his way?
He's coming. He's walking back from the yard. He said two minutes, which means five.
Ha. That's fine. Elena, this is Daniel. Daniel's our staff engineer, he's been on most of our integrations, and he's the one who's been playing with your Kent data since Tuesday night.
Hi Elena. Nice to meet you. Thanks for sending the export sample, by the way. That was really useful. I have a few questions about some of the columns, but we can get to that.
I assumed you would. Some of those columns, nobody knows what they mean. I'll answer what I can.
Ha. That's honest. There's one called ATTR_17 that I'm pretty sure is a dock door number, but it's also sometimes the word NONE, so.
It is a dock door. Sometimes. Yes.
Hey, sorry, sorry. I'm here. One of the Spokane trucks lost a mirror on a gate post this morning and I had to go look at it, which, I don't know why I had to go look at it, but I did.
No worries at all. Is the driver okay?
Driver's fine. The gate post is not fine. Anyway. It's starting, peak's starting, everything's a little bit on fire. How are you guys?
Good, good. Busy week. I drove up to Vancouver yesterday for a customer and it took me an hour to get across the bridge, so I feel your pain on everything being on fire. It's the season.
Oh, the I-5 bridge at five o'clock? That's a choice. My drivers would tell you to go around on 205, but honestly that's not much better.
Ha. Next time. Okay. So, Marcus, this is Daniel, staff engineer. Daniel, Marcus runs operations.
Hey Marcus. Good to meet you.
Hey Daniel. Tom says you're the one who's going to tell me the truth.
I'll try. That's sort of my whole job on these calls.

Ha. Okay, so just a super quick recap so Daniel has the same picture. On Tuesday we talked about 420 trucks across three terminals, routes built in spreadsheets every night, overtime at about fourteen percent of driver hours, and around forty k a month in chargebacks. Elena walked us through Samsara and the Oracle TMS, and the integration being a gate, not a score. And we're working toward a decision by October 30th with Dana. Elena, I sent the SOC 2 report Wednesday, did that come through okay?
It came through. I'm reading it. I have some questions about the exceptions section, but I'll put them in writing.

Perfect. And we've got your questionnaire, the team's working through it. So, today, Daniel's going to show Routing v3 on your Kent data, the dispatch board, constraints, and what happens when a truck goes down. Then we'll go deep on Samsara and the TMS, and then I want to talk about what a pilot looks like. Daniel, take it away.
Cool. Let me share. Can everyone see a map with a lot of colored lines on it?
Yep.

Okay. So this is the dispatch board. What you're looking at is Kent, last Tuesday, the actual orders from the export Elena sent, a hundred and thirty-eight trucks and just under fourteen hundred stops. Each color is a truck. On the left you've got the route list, one row per truck, with the driver, number of stops, total miles, and the projected end of day. Over here on the right, red means something's at risk, like a stop that's projected to miss its appointment window, or a driver who's going to run tight on hours. And I want to be upfront: I built this plan from the TMS export and the Samsara data, I did not have your dispatchers' tribal knowledge, so there's going to be stuff in here that's wrong in ways only Ray would know.
Ray would have opinions. Yeah. How many reds are there?

Right now, eleven. Mostly two DCs in Sumner where the appointment windows were really tight. And honestly, I'd guess your dispatchers already know those. For comparison, when I took the routes your team actually ran that night and scored them the same way, it was thirty-one reds, and about nine percent more miles. But again, salt. I'm comparing a plan to a plan, not to what actually happened on the road.
No, that's fair. Thirty-one feels about right, honestly. Tuesday was a bad night.

So let me show constraints, because that's usually where these things fall apart. If I click into a driver, say this guy, truck 2214. You can see his hours-of-service clock. That's coming straight from Samsara, so it's his actual remaining drive time and on-duty time, not an estimate. The solver treats that as a hard constraint. It will not build a route that puts him over, period. If the only way to cover a stop is to break someone's hours, it leaves the stop unassigned and flags it for a human.
Okay, wait. That's a big one. So it would rather leave a stop on the table than blow someone's hours.

Yes. By default. You can configure how much overtime you're willing to spend before it does that, like, allow up to an hour of overtime per driver if it saves a late delivery at a priority customer. But hours of service itself, the federal limit, is never negotiable in the solver.
Huh. Okay. I like that it asks a person instead of just quietly doing the dumb thing.

Then dock windows. So every stop has its appointment window from the TMS, but you can also set location rules. This is the part I think Ray will care about. Say this DC in Sumner, everyone knows dock wait is forty-five minutes on Tuesday mornings. You can set that here, service time forty-five minutes, Tuesdays, six to ten. And then every route that touches it accounts for it. You set it once and it sticks, instead of living in someone's head.
Where does that data live? The location rules. Is that in your system or does it need to go back into the TMS?
In ours. We don't write back to the TMS, at least not in what I'm proposing. That's a good question though, I'll come back to it in the integration part.
Okay.

And then over time, the ETA model learns dock waits on its own from the Samsara geofences. That's Kenji's model, our ML engineer. It's gone from about six minutes of average error down to a bit over four this year. I'll be honest that dock wait time is still the hardest part for it, so for a while the manual rules are going to beat the model at your worst DCs. That's sort of why we let you override it.
Daniel, show them the lock thing.

Yeah. So, Marcus, you said on Tuesday, or Tom told me you said, that dispatchers want to override. So, a dispatcher can drag a stop from one truck to another, like this, and the board re-scores it instantly. If they like a route, they lock it, this padlock, and the solver will never touch it again. Everything else re-plans around the locked routes. So it's not all or nothing.
Can you lock part of a route? Like, these first three stops are sacred because the driver has a relationship with the receiver, but do whatever you want after?
Yes. You can lock a sequence. That's actually a common one. Grocery fleets do it all the time for their morning stores.
Okay. That's good. That's actually really good.

So now the fun part. Let's say it's 9:40 in the morning, and truck 2231 breaks down. Fuel pump, whatever. He's in Auburn, he's got eight stops left. So I'm going to mark the truck down. Right-click, out of service. And what happens now is the solver re-plans every unlocked route in the terminal, with everybody's current positions from Samsara, their remaining hours, and all the remaining windows. That's about four hundred stops still open at this point in the day. And, there. Done.
Wait, that's it?

That's it. About four seconds for four hundred stops. It's in the corner there, 4.1 seconds. And you can see what it did. It split his eight stops across three trucks. Two of them were already nearby. And the one it flagged, this yellow one, is a driver who'll end up about twenty minutes into overtime, so it's asking the dispatcher, do you approve this or not. The dispatcher hits accept, and the new stops push to the drivers.

Okay. So, that's — I mean, today that's forty-five minutes of my lead on the phone. Minimum. And he'd probably have ended up giving all eight stops to one guy, because that's one phone call instead of three.
And that one guy is your overtime.

And that one guy is my overtime. Yeah. Okay. I'm just thinking out loud here. The part I'm trying to picture is what Ray does when he disagrees with it. Like, it splits the stops across three trucks, and Ray looks at it and goes, no, that driver's slow on residential, or that guy's truck doesn't have a liftgate. What does he do?

Two things. In the moment, he just drags the stop where he wants it and locks it, and the solver re-plans around his decision. Takes a second. And then longer term, the liftgate thing, that's a vehicle attribute. You tag the truck as no liftgate, you tag the stop as needs liftgate, and the solver never makes that mistake again. Driver preferences we can do too, but I'd start with the hard stuff like equipment.
Okay. That's the answer I wanted. If Ray feels like he's the boss of it, he'll use it.
Daniel, can you show the end-of-day view too? I think that's the screen Dana's going to care about.

Yeah, quickly. So this is the day report. Planned versus actual for every route, miles, on-time at each appointment, and overtime by driver, pulled from the Samsara hours. You can roll it up by week or by terminal. For a pilot, this is where you'd compare the sixty pilot trucks against the rest of Kent. You can export it to a spreadsheet, so your finance people can check our math instead of trusting a dashboard.
Yeah. That's the Dana screen. Can it show chargeback exposure? Like, late at a retailer with a penalty program?

Not chargebacks directly, we don't have your penalty rules. But if you tag which customers have on-time programs, it'll report late arrivals for just those, and you can apply your own rates in the spreadsheet. That's probably more honest anyway.
Fine by me. I'd rather apply the rates myself.
Sorry, going back a second. How does the new route get to the driver? You said push. Push to what?

Today, two options. Our driver app, or, because I know you don't want another app, we can push to the Samsara driver app through their routing API. The stops just show up in the app they already have. That's how two of our beta fleets do it.
Okay. That is the right answer. I was ready to argue.
Ha. We did our homework.
Is this live, though? Like, is this what your customers are running today, or is this the next version?

Good question. This is Routing v3. It's in beta with six fleets, since September 8th. General availability is November 17th. Across the beta fleets so far we're seeing about eleven percent fewer miles, and on-time going from 91.2 to 94.6 percent. So, real, running on real trucks every day, but not GA yet. A pilot for you would start on the beta and roll onto GA in the middle.
So we'd be piloting beta software.

Yes. I'm not going to pretend otherwise. The solver itself has been stable. What's still moving is mostly UI polish and some of the reporting. If that's a problem for your security review I'd rather know now.
It's not a problem by itself. I need to know which version we are being reviewed against. Put it in the questionnaire answers.
Will do.
Elena, I know you've been waiting for this part. Daniel, do you want to talk Samsara first and then the TMS?

Yeah. Samsara's the easy one, so let's get it out of the way. We connect through their API with a token that you generate on your side, scoped read-only for vehicle locations and hours of service, plus write for routes if you want the push to their driver app. We pull location every thirty seconds and HOS clocks every couple of minutes. Nothing gets installed on the trucks. It's the same integration that's running with our beta fleets today, and if your token gets revoked we just stop seeing data. There's no other access.
Rate limits? We already have two internal dashboards hitting that API.

Good question. At 420 trucks we're well under their limits, but I'd want to look at what your dashboards are pulling so we're not stepping on each other. If you can tell me roughly how often they poll, I'll do the math. Worst case we slow our location polling to a minute, which is fine for routing.
Okay. I'll check. Now the TMS.

Now the TMS. So, I looked at the export sample and the version details you sent, and I want to be really straightforward here, because I think you've heard some soft answers. There's no API, and nothing inbound, so there are basically two options, and they have real trade-offs. Option one is a nightly SFTP batch. Your TMS already produces the finance export, we'd add a second export job with orders, appointments and the location fields, and push it outbound to an SFTP endpoint on our side. We validate it, and if the file's late or malformed, it pages someone, on our side and yours. That works with what you have today. No change board, I think, because it's outbound.
Probably no change board. A new scheduled export job, I can do that myself.

Great. The downside is it's a snapshot. It's whatever was in the TMS at the cutoff. Marcus said on Tuesday maybe ten percent of orders change after that. With the batch, those changes don't flow in automatically. A dispatcher would either update the stop in our board directly, or you'd do a second, smaller drop mid-morning. That's manual-ish. It's the honest version.
And option two.

Option two is a middleware connector. A small service that runs inside your network, on a VM you control, reads the database views you already have access to, and sends changes outbound to us over HTTPS every minute or so. So it's near real-time, appointment changes show up on the dispatch board without anyone touching them. The trade-offs are, one, it's software installed inside your data center, so I'm assuming that's your change board. Two, those views on a customized 2014 Oracle install, I'd want a couple of weeks to map them properly, especially the custom fields. Realistically four to six weeks to do it well. And three, it's another thing to maintain. If someone changes a view, it breaks, and we have to fix it.
The change board meets on the third Thursday. So the next one is October 15th. If I submit something, the earliest install is after that.

Right. So, my honest recommendation, and Elena, push back on this. Pilot on the SFTP batch. It's enough to prove the routing, and dispatchers can handle the ten percent by hand on sixty trucks. In parallel, if the pilot looks good, we start the middleware connector so it's ready for the full rollout. I would not try to do the connector before the pilot. It'll eat your whole decision window.
Hm. That is a reasonable answer. I don't love the manual part. But I'd rather hear it now than discover it in week three.
Ten percent of sixty trucks is, what, call it sixty stops a day? Seventy? Ray already re-keys more than that. That's not the thing that kills this.
For the pilot. For 420 trucks it is the thing that kills it. So the connector has to be real, not a slide.

Agreed. And I'm not going to tell you we have one sitting on a shelf for your exact version. We've done this pattern for two other on-prem TMS installs, neither of them Oracle. I can share the architecture doc for one of those this week so you can see what you'd be approving.
Yes. Send that. And the file spec for the batch, so I can see what fields you need.
Will do, both.
One more thing, and I'm sorry, Tom, I know this is a sales call. You had an outage last week. Thursday. Your ETA service was down for, I think, forty-seven minutes. I read your status page.
No, that's fair. Daniel, do you want to take that?

Yeah. Forty-seven minutes is right. A Redis cluster failed over, and our dispatch workers retried way too aggressively, it turned into a retry storm and the ETA service fell over. About three hundred fleets saw stale ETAs. The thing I'm least proud of is the status page. It took us twenty-six minutes to update it, which is too slow, and we know it. We're fixing the retry behavior and the status page process. I can send you the post-mortem once it's final.
Please send it. I'm less worried about the outage than about the twenty-six minutes. If my dispatchers are planning off stale data, I need to know immediately.
Completely fair. That's the exact feedback we're taking from it.

Okay. So let me switch to the commercial side for a few minutes, because I know we're working back from October 30th. Our list price for Routing v3 is sixty-eight dollars per truck per month. That includes the dispatch board, the Samsara integration, the ETA model, and integration support from Daniel's team. What I'd like to propose is a pilot. Sixty trucks, out of Kent, for six weeks, at no cost. And if it hits the numbers we agree on up front, it converts to the full fleet at sixty-two a truck instead of sixty-eight.
Sixty-two. Okay.
Sixty-two, on a two-year term.

I mean, I appreciate the free pilot, that genuinely helps me with Dana. But I'll say the obvious thing, which is RouteWise is at fifty-two. So you're still ten bucks a truck over them, at the discount. That's, um, what is that, four-twenty times ten times twelve, it's fifty grand a year, about. Dana will do that math before I finish the sentence.

Yeah, she will, and she should. Here's how I'd frame it to her. Fifty k a year is a bit more than one month of your chargebacks. If the pilot shows we cut even a quarter of the chargebacks and a few points of overtime, the difference pays for itself several times over. And RouteWise has to actually integrate with your TMS, which, Elena, correct me, they haven't shown yet.
They have not. They sent a brochure on Tuesday. It does not mention our version.

Okay. Look, I'm not trying to beat you up on price on this call. I just need you to know the number's in the room. If the pilot's great, I can sell sixty-two. If it's fine, I'm going to lose that argument to fifty-two.
Totally understood. And that's fair. That's exactly why we want the pilot to be measured on your numbers.
And the timing, help me think about this. Six weeks from, what, when would it even start? If we start in two weeks, six weeks is the end of November. Dana's decision is the 30th.

Right. So, what we've done before is, the formal read-out happens at week three, with on-time and overtime data, which you said shows up fast. Dana decides on the 30th off that. The contract's signed with a clause that says if weeks four through six fall apart, you can walk. So you're not betting on three weeks blind.
Hm. Okay. That could work. She'll want that clause in writing, not in an email from you.

It'll be in the proposal. And let me say what I'd put in for success metrics, so you can react now instead of in a document. Three numbers on the sixty pilot trucks, against the same trucks over the six weeks before the pilot. One, on-time arrival at DC appointments, specifically at the customers with on-time programs. Two, overtime hours per driver, from your payroll, not our report. Three, miles per stop. And then a softer one, which is how late the dispatchers are staying, because I think that matters to you even if it doesn't show up in Dana's spreadsheet.

No, that's good. That's actually close to what I'd write. I'd swap miles per stop for fuel, maybe, because Dana sees the fuel bill and she doesn't see miles. But we can get fuel off Samsara, right, Elena?
Roughly. Idle time and fuel used per vehicle, yes. It's not perfect, but it's consistent.
Great, fuel instead of miles then. And what's the bar? What does on-time have to move by for you to call it a win?

Ugh, now you're asking me to commit. Um. Okay, I'm thinking out loud. If on-time at the program customers goes up four or five points, and overtime on those trucks drops by a third, I'd call that a win, and I think Dana would. Less than that and it's a conversation. Put that in and I'll tell you if she flinches.
Done. Four to five points on-time, a third off overtime. I'll put those in as the targets.

Okay. Then the thing I keep coming back to. The live ETA. Tuesday you said it's on the roadmap for this quarter. I've been thinking about it since, and honestly, if I'm going to Dana, I need to know when. Like a month. Is it December? Is it January? Because that's what gets my dispatchers off the phone. Daniel, you're the engineer. When?

Yeah. Um. So, I'm going to be careful here, and I'm sorry, I know that's not what you want. The pieces under it exist. The ETA model is the same one you saw, and we have live locations from Samsara. But the customer-facing link itself is real work, and it's competing with some other things for the same engineers this quarter. I'd want to check with Maya, she runs the routing team, before I give you a date. I don't want to give you one that I'm making up on a call.
Okay. I respect that, honestly. But I do need a date.

And you'll have one. Look, it's a priority for us, and you're a big part of why. Let me get together with Maya and Daniel, and we'll get you something concrete next week. Not a vague roadmap slide. An actual answer.
Next week. Okay. I'm going to hold you to that.
Please do.
And the requirement from Tuesday still stands. Samsara GPS, no new driver app.
Yep, I've got that written down. Any design we do for you would work off the Samsara locations.

Okay, let's lock next steps, I know we're at time. On our side, we'll get the completed security questionnaire back to you, Elena. I'm aiming for end of next week, along with the beta version note you asked for. Daniel sends the batch file spec and the connector architecture doc, and the post-mortem when it's final. I'll send a written pilot proposal by Tuesday, October 6th, with the sixty trucks, the six weeks, the success metrics, the sixty-two conversion and the walk-away clause. And the live ETA answer next week.
The questionnaire by the ninth would be good. I need time to read it before legal touches anything.

By the ninth. Done. Oh, and Elena, one from Tuesday. Asher confirmed SCIM is supported on the enterprise plan, so provisioning can come straight from your Okta groups. I'll put that in writing in the questionnaire too.
Good. Thank you.

And on my side, I'll brief Dana. Probably Monday, she's out tomorrow. I'll tell her what I saw today, honestly, the re-plan thing is going to be the part I lead with. And I'll get Ray to watch the recording. If Ray likes the locks, I'm halfway there.
If Ray wants to poke at it himself, I'm happy to do a thirty-minute session with him on the Kent data. No sales, just him breaking it.
Oh, he'd love that. He'd love breaking it. Okay, let me set that up.
Great. Thank you both. Really good session.
Yeah, good stuff. Thanks Daniel. Thanks Tom.
Thank you. Send me the documents.
Will do. Thanks, everyone.

general.tldr: Daniel's Routing v3 demo on Harbor & Pine's own Kent data landed well, especially the 4-second re-plan. Tom offered a free 60-truck, 6-week pilot converting at $62/truck (vs RouteWise at $52). Live ETA still has no date: Daniel deferred to Maya, and Tom promised something concrete next week.

items.text: Show Routing v3 on Harbor & Pine's real Kent orders, work through the Samsara and Oracle TMS integration with Elena, and put pilot terms on the table ahead of the Oct 30 decision.
On last Tuesday's Kent orders (138 trucks, ~1,400 stops), v3's plan had 11 at-risk stops vs 31 for the dispatchers' plan, with ~9% fewer miles. Daniel cautioned this is plan-vs-plan only.
A simulated breakdown re-planned ~400 open stops in 4.1 seconds. Marcus said the same re-plan takes his lead at least 45 minutes on the phone today.
TMS: pilot on a nightly SFTP batch and build a middleware connector in parallel for full rollout (4–6 weeks, needs the Oct 15 change board).
Pricing: $68/truck/month list; free 6-week pilot on 60 Kent trucks, converting at $62 on a two-year term. Marcus flagged RouteWise at $52, about $50k/yr less.
Live ETA still has no date. Daniel won't commit without Maya, and Tom promised 'something concrete next week'.
Hours of service from Samsara is a hard constraint: the solver leaves a stop unassigned rather than break a driver's legal limit. Overtime allowance is configurable.
Location rules (e.g. 45-minute Tuesday dock waits in Sumner) are set once in Tandem. Kenji's ETA model learns dock waits over time but still struggles with them.
Dispatchers can drag, lock whole routes or lock stop sequences. Vehicle attributes like liftgate prevent repeat mistakes.
The day report shows planned vs actual, on-time by appointment and overtime by driver, with spreadsheet export. Marcus called it 'the Dana screen'.
Routes can push to the existing Samsara driver app, so no new app is needed.
Samsara: read-only API token, 30-second location polling; rate limits to be checked against H&P's two internal dashboards.
SFTP batch is outbound-only and Elena can set it up herself, but it's a cutoff snapshot that misses the ~10% of orders that change intraday.
Middleware connector is near real-time but runs inside H&P's network, needs change-board approval and mapping of custom views. Tandem has built this for two on-prem TMSs, neither Oracle.
Elena raised the Sep 24 ETA outage (47 min). Her bigger concern is the 26 minutes it took to update the status page.
Read-out at week three so Dana can decide by Oct 30. Walk-away clause if weeks 4–6 fall apart, in writing.
Success targets: on-time at program customers up 4–5 points and overtime on pilot trucks down a third. Also track fuel (from Samsara) and dispatcher hours.
Written pilot proposal by Tue Oct 6.
Completed security questionnaire back to Elena by Oct 9.
Batch file spec, connector architecture doc and outage post-mortem to Elena.
Marcus briefs Dana on Monday and sets up a hands-on session for Ray with Daniel.

demo.tldr: The live re-plan and dispatcher locks won Marcus over. Elena accepted the SFTP-first plan for the pilot but needs a real connector for 420 trucks. Price and the missing live ETA date are the open objections.

highlights.title: Truck breakdown re-planned: 400 stops in 4 seconds
Daniel's honest take on the Oracle TMS: SFTP for the pilot, connector for rollout
$68 list, free 60-truck pilot at $62; Marcus counters with RouteWise at $52
No live ETA date: Daniel defers to Maya, Tom promises an answer next week

ask.q: What did we say about live ETA?
ask.a: Marcus pressed for an actual month, reminding Tom he'd said 'this quarter' on Tuesday. Daniel wouldn't give a date: the pieces exist, but the customer-facing link is real work competing for the same engineers, and he wants to check with Maya first. Tom promised 'something concrete next week', and Marcus said he'd hold him to it.

ask.q: How do we compare to RouteWise?
ask.a: RouteWise is $52/truck/month against Tandem's $62 pilot conversion, about $50k/yr more for 420 trucks. Tom framed that as roughly one month of H&P's chargebacks, and Elena noted RouteWise still hasn't shown support for her Oracle version. Marcus said he can sell $62 if the pilot is great but will lose to $52 if it's only fine.

60 trucks out of Kent for 6 weeks at no cost, converting to the full fleet at $62/truck/month (list $68) on a two-year term. A week-three read-out lets Dana decide by Oct 30, and a written walk-away clause covers weeks 4–6. Targets: on-time at program customers up 4–5 points and overtime down a third, with fuel and dispatcher hours also tracked.

ask.q: How will the Oracle TMS integration work?
ask.a: There are two options. A nightly outbound SFTP batch Elena can set up herself, which misses intraday changes, or a middleware connector inside H&P's network that is near real-time but needs the Oct 15 change board and 4–6 weeks of work. Daniel recommended piloting on SFTP and building the connector in parallel. Elena agreed for the pilot but said the connector must be real for 420 trucks.

ask.q: What did Daniel show in the demo?
ask.a: Routing v3 on H&P's own Kent orders (138 trucks, ~1,400 stops): the dispatch board with at-risk flags, hard hours-of-service constraints, dock-window rules, dispatcher locks, and a breakdown re-plan of ~400 stops in 4.1 seconds. He also showed the end-of-day planned-vs-actual report and pushing routes into the Samsara driver app.

ask.q: What would make the pilot a win for Marcus?
ask.a: On-time at customers with on-time programs up 4–5 points and overtime on the pilot trucks down by a third, measured against the same trucks' prior six weeks using H&P payroll data. Below that, he says, 'it's a conversation'.
